Where it began

Javagal Srinath was born in Mysore on 31 August 1969 and played cricket from an early age. He also studied hard enough to earn a degree in instrumentation engineering from the Sri Jayachamarajendra College of Engineering in his home city. Not many fast bowlers can explain the workings of a speed gun as well as trouble it.

Gundappa Viswanath, then a Karnataka selector, noticed him in a club match. On his first-class debut, against Hyderabad in 1989–90, Srinath took a hat-trick in his first innings with the ball and two wickets in two balls in his second. He finished that first season with 25 wickets from six games.

The player

He made his one-day debut at Sharjah in 1991 and his Test debut at Brisbane on the tour of Australia that followed. Indian pitches of the time favoured spin, so for a while he spent home Tests watching. That changed after Kapil Dev retired in 1994. In his first home Test, against West Indies, Srinath took five wickets, made 60 with the bat and was named player of the match.

In 67 Tests from 1991 to 2002 he took 236 wickets at 30.47, with ten five-wicket innings, a ten-wicket match and a best of 8 for 86. Before him, Kapil Dev was the only Indian fast bowler with 200 Test wickets. In one-day cricket he took 315 wickets, played in four World Cups and was in the side that shared the 2002 Champions Trophy. In England he had a fine summer with Gloucestershire in 1995, taking 87 wickets, including 9 for 76 against Glamorgan.

What made him special

Pace, honest and hard. One of his deliveries in the 1997–98 series against Australia was clocked at 149.6 kilometres an hour, and Alistair Campbell of Zimbabwe reckoned him quicker than Allan Donald or Lance Klusener at their best. Imran Khan thought nobody anywhere was more underrated. He could reverse the old ball, too, so for all the talk of dry, slow pitches, his average at home was better than his average abroad.

For years he was India's only regular fast bowler, a heavy load to carry. An injury in 1997 kept him out for months, yet he came back to have the best year of his career in 1998. With the bat he made four Test fifties, the best of them 76, though the hundred he deserved for all that hard work never quite turned up.

Away from the middle

He received the Arjuna Award in 1999 and an honorary doctorate from the University of Mysore in 2023. After playing he toured England with the Lashings World XI, spent time in the commentary box and, from 2006, became an international match referee, a role that took him to the 2007 World Cup, this time with a notebook instead of a ball.

And finally

Srinath had wanted to give up one-day cricket before the 2003 World Cup, but Sourav Ganguly asked him to stay on for one more tournament. He stayed, and India went all the way to the final. Not every postponed retirement turns out so well.
